title: Mohnish Pabrai's Session at The Investor’s Podcast on April 1, 2024
summary: A life-focused 'train ride' conversation with Stig Brodersen in which Pabrai discusses how early financial independence freed him, why managing outside money has never been stressful, and how he deliberately engineers happiness and relationships (his 'Chai with Pabrai' teas, Buffett's harsh filter for people). He also covers owning Reysas like a private family business, his no-notes reading habit, his track record versus the S&P, Boeing as a case of short-termism, and how Dakshana and his Buffett lunch show that action lets luck do its part.

ideas.idea: The main value of wealth is independence: after selling a TransTech stake, he fired himself as CEO of his IT company to spend time on what gave him the most satisfaction.
ideas.detail: Turning about $1 million after tax into roughly $13 million in five years made him financially independent at 33; relationships did not change, but how he spent his days did. He credits Munger's view that independence was the main driver for wealth.

ideas.idea: Managing other people's money has never been stressful; the only sadness is investors who came in at the peak and redeemed at the bottom.
ideas.detail: In the financial crisis the funds fell 65-67% from the peak versus about 40% for the index, and AUM went from about $600 million to $200 million, yet most money stayed. Managing money also brought friendships and better access to companies.

ideas.idea: He still keeps an intrinsic-value spreadsheet of his holdings as a beacon, updating it periodically since there are only one or two new ideas a year.
ideas.detail: It was a rope out of the well during the financial crisis; now it helps educate investors in a concentrated Turkish position that redeeming means selling at market value, not intrinsic value.

ideas.idea: He owns about a third of Reysas in Turkey and treats it like a private family business he wants to own forever.
ideas.detail: As long as the founding family keeps its ownership and runs the business, he wants no changes; once you own part of a truly wonderful business bought at a wonderful price, you are done and just watch the paint dry.

ideas.idea: Kicking the tires by visiting plants, coal mines, terminals and warehouses has been a big improvement; being an armchair investor makes you miss a lot.
ideas.detail: He regrets not doing more field visits earlier; the travel has a huge payoff in understanding the businesses he owns.

ideas.idea: Happiness requires taking the bull by the horns: constantly ask whether you are content and change what is out of alignment.
ideas.detail: Only two or three single-digit years out of 42 since age 18 were bad, and each led to a change such as moving from engineering to marketing at Tellabs or leaving TransTech, which produced new highs.

ideas.idea: Deliberately grow deep relationships and de-emphasize the ones that do not, rather than drifting through life out of loyalty.
ideas.detail: His 'Chai with Pabrai' Assam teas in Austin a couple of times a month have produced only a small number of deep friendships out of dozens of meetings, but he is fine with a low ratio; his father said one good wife and one good friend is all you need.

ideas.idea: Apply Buffett's harsh filter to people: engage only the 3-4% who are clearly exceptional and lump the unknown 92% with the bad, because there are no called strikes and letting the wrong person in is costly.
ideas.detail: At their lunch Buffett said he is not a great judge of humans but in a 100-person cocktail party he can spot three or four wonderful people and three or four to avoid; there is little cost to missing a great individual since future teas are infinite.

ideas.idea: Choose truth over diplomacy and be direct when saying no; people appreciate candor more than excuses.
ideas.detail: Citing Power vs Force, he says not being candid is a disservice; when he declined a dinner invitation directly the person responded graciously.

ideas.idea: He prefers bridge over poker because bridge has zero luck and is purely skill; investing similarly is dominated by probabilities.
ideas.detail: He plays four to six hours of bridge a week, Buffett plays 10-15 hours; Buffett did terribly at a poker tournament and went back to bridge. He played small-stakes social bridge with Munger for $100-150.

ideas.idea: Trust, reliability, integrity, honesty, hard work and fairness are the principles that carry the most weight, and being trustable is a long, infinite game.
ideas.detail: Munger calls McDonald's one of the best educational institutions because it teaches young workers reliability; an intern who showed up only 60% of the time did not grasp its importance.

ideas.idea: Few people live by these simple principles because the payoffs come decades later and there is no visible X-leads-to-Y relationship.
ideas.detail: Buffett was not well known outside the US until 15-20 years ago; the used-car-dealer transactional mindset leads to the shallows of life.

ideas.idea: Boeing shows what happens when bean counters replace engineers and stop playing the long game.
ideas.detail: After the McDonnell Douglas merger, management forced huge engines and a stretched fuselage onto the old 737 instead of an 8-10 year, multi-billion clean-sheet design, leading to the two MAX crashes; with only two aircraft makers, the world needs Boeing to be engineer-driven.

ideas.idea: He has never taken notes in class or from books in 60 years, and neither did Buffett when studying Lehman Brothers.
ideas.detail: Tracy Britt found fewer than five words of notes in the Lehman 10-Ks Buffett read during the crisis; when the SEC asked Berkshire for staff notes on an acquisition, Munger replied there is no staff and there are no notes.

ideas.idea: From 1994-95 through 2018 he beat the S&P over every period, lagged from 2018 to 2020, and has been beating it again since 2020.
ideas.detail: Outcomes come down to a sliver of individual names; he has changed some approaches over the years and expects to be back ahead over all periods after a few more years.

ideas.idea: Sidestepping the dot-com bubble was partly luck from a front-row seat via private investments, while he failed to see the 2008 crisis coming and had positions go to zero.
ideas.detail: Quoting Munger, 'we are old too soon and wise too late'; he does not dwell on luck and focuses on the positions and opportunities actually in front of him.

ideas.idea: A guaranteed 20% compounding account would be tempting enough that he might take it and go all in on bridge.
ideas.detail: An investor who shorted Berkshire at $70,000 a share also regretted not buying 18% 30-year US Treasuries in 1980-81, which would have compounded with no volatility for 30 years.

ideas.idea: Not believing in large inheritances forces you to give money away; Dakshana was built only because the model's originator would not scale, so he cloned it.
ideas.detail: Started in 2006-2007 with the intention of just writing checks, Dakshana blew away his most optimistic goals and enriched his life; today he would give to one or two nonprofits that do a good job if they could absorb the amounts.

ideas.idea: Take actions so that luck can do its part; the universe conspires to help good people who work hard and play the infinite game.
ideas.detail: He was willing to pay up to $2 million (2-3% of his net worth) for the Buffett lunch purely to say thank you; it led to a friendship with Munger and 'infinite lunches free'. He calls himself Forrest Gump for stumbling into these things.

ideas.idea: Being a giver does not require wealth; Dakshana's poor scholars give their time, and reliable, honest, high-integrity people almost never do terribly in life.
ideas.detail: His rebuttal to skeptics of Dakshana's 'give, give, give' model is that it is hard to find examples of very reliable, hardworking, high-integrity people who failed.
